Submission received: 2 September 2024 / Revised: 28 October 2024 / Accepted: 29 October 2024 / Published: 5 November 2024 Abstract Skin diseases are a common health problem affecting millions of people worldwide. Effective treatment often depends on the precise delivery of drugs to the affected areas. One promising approach is currently the transdermal drug delivery system (TDDS), whose significant challenge is the poor penetration of many compounds into the skin due to the stratum corneum (SC), which acts as a formidable barrier. To overcome this limitation, nanocarriers have emerged as a highly effective alternative. This review discusses the use of liposomes and ethosomes for transdermal drug delivery. Liposomes are micro- or nanostructures consisting of a lipid bilayer surrounding an aqueous core. They facilitate transdermal drug penetration and may be advantageous for site-specific targeting. Some methods of treating skin diseases involve incorporating drugs such as acyclovir, dithranol, and tretinoin or bioactive compounds such as fluconazole, melanin, glycolic acid, kojic acid, and CoQ10 into nanocarriers. The inability of liposomes to pass through the narrowed intercellular channels of the stratum corneum led to the invention of lipid-based vesicular systems such as ethosomes. They are structurally similar to conventional liposomes, as they are prepared from phospholipids, but they contain a high ethanol concentration. Ethosomes are noninvasive carriers that allow drugs to reach the deep layers of the skin. Examples of commonly used substances and drugs combined with ethosomes in cosmetics include methotrexate, ascorbic acid, vitamin A and E, and colchicine. A significant development in this area is the use of rutin-loaded ethosomes. Encapsulating rutin in ethosomes significantly improves its stability and enhances skin penetration, allowing more efficient delivery to deeper skin layers. In cosmetics, rutin–ethosome formulations are used to protect the skin from oxidative stress, reduce redness, and improve capillary strength, making it a valuable formulation in anti-aging and anti-inflammatory products. The results of the first clinical trial of the acyclovir–ethosome formulation confirm that ethosomes require further investigation. The work provides an update on recent advances in pharmaceutical and cosmetic applications, mentioning the essential points of commercially available formulations, clinical trials, and patents in the recent past. 1. Introduction The skin, one of the largest organs of the human body, constantly acts as a self-regulating barrier that protects against water loss and stabilizes both the internal and external environment. When healthy, it acts as a natural shield, but when it succumbs to illness, its defense functions are weakened. Small particles and microorganisms can then penetrate the stratum corneum more easily, and valuable nutrients such as water and electrolytes are lost more quickly. Changes in lifestyle and the environment have contributed to an increase in skin diseases in recent years [1,2]. The treatment of dermatological conditions mainly involves pharmacotherapy and physiotherapy. Transdermal drug delivery has significant advantages over oral methods and injections, as it delivers active ingredients directly to the damaged tissues where symptoms occur. New drug delivery methods have been developed to improve efficacy, stability, and protection in response to these challenges. A breakthrough has been the transdermal drug delivery system (TDDS), which enables effective absorption of active ingredients through the skin. According to studies, more than 70% of patients and physicians choose TDDS to treat dermatological diseases [3]. This method has many advantages, such as direct action on the skin, bypassing the first-pass effect through the liver, high bioavailability, maintaining stable drug concentrations in the blood, low incidence of side effects, and the possibility of rapid discontinuation of therapy. However, the main obstacle to using TDDS is the presence of an impermeable outer layer of skin, which impedes the penetration of active substances. The stratum corneum (SC) comprises flat, keratinized cells and is the main barrier to the active ingredients of cosmetics and drugs [4,5]. To overcome this barrier, several carriers in which small amounts of active ingredients are encapsulated have begun to be developed [6]. Modification of drugs and other active ingredients at the nanoscale significantly improves their therapeutic efficacy and reduces the risk of side effects. One solution for increasing the permeation of drugs and cosmetic substances is vesicular systems such as liposomes and ethosomes. In recent years, topical drug delivery in the form of liposomes has become increasingly popular [7]. Deformable liposomes were the first generation of flexible vesicles that could penetrate the intact skin barrier. These lipid-rich vesicles are believed to transport a significant amount of drugs through the skin, increasing their systemic absorption. However, classical liposomes cannot penetrate deeply into the skin due to their large particle size, high manufacturing costs, and low stability. fetched_contents.text: Therapeutic and cosmeceutical potential of ethosomes: An overview Abstract The main disadvantage of transdermal drug delivery is the poor penetration of most compounds into the human skin. The main barrier of the skin is located within its uppermost layer, the stratum corneum (SC). Several approaches have been developed to weaken this skin barrier. One of the approaches for increasing the skin penetration of drugs and many cosmetic chemicals is the use of vesicular systems, such as, liposomes and ethosomes. Ethosomes are phospholipid-based elastic nanovesicles containing a high content of ethanol (20–45%). Ethanol is known as an efficient permeation enhancer and has been added in the vesicular systems to prepare elastic nanovesicles. It can interact with the polar head group region of the lipid molecules, resulting in the reduction of the melting point of the stratum corneum lipid, thereby increasing lipid fluidity and cell membrane permeability. The high flexibility of vesicular membranes from the added ethanol permits the elastic vesicles to squeeze themselves through the pores, which are much smaller than their diameters. Ethosomal systems are much more efficient in delivering substances to the skin in the terms of quantity and depth, than either conventional liposomes or hydroalcoholic solutions. The scope of this small review is to introduce the novel concept of ethosomes and to describe some approaches and mechanisms of stimulating topical and transdermal products with ethosomes. Keywords: Ethosomes, liposomes, novel drug delivery, penetration enhancer, Percutaneous absorption INTRODUCTION Human skin is an effective, selective barrier to chemical permeation, although the skin as a route for delivery can offer many advantages, including avoidance of first-pass metabolism, lower fluctuations in plasma drug levels, targeting of the active ingredient for a local effect, and good patient compliance.[1] Water soluble molecules and drugs are normally not able to cross the skin as the skin is a natural barrier to water. The stratum corneum is composed of insoluble bundled keratins surrounded by a cell envelope, stabilized by cross-linked proteins and covalently bound lipids as shown in Figure 1. In general, the epidermis (specifically the stratum corneum) provides the major control element; most small, water-soluble, and non-electrolytes diffuse into the systemic circulation a thousand times more rapidly when the horny layer is present.[2] Thus, to maximise the flux of the drug, the barrier hinderance is reduced by various approaches. Several technological advances have been made in the recent decades to overcome skin barrier properties. Examples include physical means such as iontophoresis, sonophoresis, microneedles, and chemical means, using penetration enhancers and biochemical means, such as, liposomal vesicles and enzyme inhibition. The physical means like iontophoresis, microneedles, and sonophoresis are relatively complicated to use, and will affect patient compliance.[3] The use of chemical enhancers such as surfactants and organic solvents induce irritation, cause damage, and reduce skin barrier function, therefore, it is desirable to deliver the therapeutic agents that maintain the normal skin barrier function without the aid of a chemical enhancer.[4] One such approach is the use of vesicular systems. In the past decade, topical delivery of drugs by liposomal formulation has evoked considerable interest. Deformable liposomes[5] and transferosomes were the first generation of elastic vesicles introduced by Ceve and Blume, in 1992, and were reported to penetrate intact skin while carrying a therapeutic concentration of drugs, when applied under nonoccluded conditions.[6] The drug, encapsulated in lipid vesicles, prepared from phospholipids and nonionic surfactants is known to be transported into and across the skin. The lipids present in the skin contribute to the barrier properties of the skin and prevent the systemic absorption of drugs. Due to the amphiphilic nature, lipid vesicles may serve as non-toxic penetration enhancers for drugs.[7] In addition, the vesicles can be used for encapsulating hydrophilic and lipophilic as well as low and high molecular weight drugs. Therefore, these lipid rich vesicles are hypothesized to carry a significant quantity of drugs across the skin, thus enhancing the systemic absorption of drugs.[8] The use of lipid vesicles in the delivery system for skin treatment has attracted increasing attention in recent years, however, it is generally agreed that classic liposomes are of little or no value as carriers for drug delivery, because they do not penetrate the skin deeply, but rather remain confined to the upper layer of the stratum corneum; only specifically designed vesicles are shown to enhance permeation into the stratum corneum barrier. It has been investigated and reported that lipid vesicular systems embodying ethanol in relatively high concentrations, called ethosomes, are very efficient at enhancing the skin permeation of a number of drugs.[9] ETHOSOMES Ethosomes were developed by Touitou et al.,1997, as additional novel lipid carriers composed of ethanol, phospholipids, and water. They are reported to improve the skin delivery of various drugs.[10] Ethanol is an efficient permeation enhancer that is believed to act by affecting the intercellular region of the stratum corneum. node_outputs.N9:
Mechanistic reasons why ethosomes may improve skin permeation

Ethisomes differ from conventional liposomes primarily by their structural composition and flexibility. Ethosomes are phospholipid-based elastic nanovesicles containing a high ethanol concentration, whereas conventional liposomes are rigid bilayer vesicles without such a high ethanol component [N1-F1][N4-R2]. This structural difference is central to their permeation behavior: ethosomes are described as “more flexible and adaptable than typical liposomes, which have restricted penetration because of their rigid bilayer” [N4-R1], and the high ethanol content makes ethosomes unique by disturbing skin lipid structure and increasing membrane fluidity [N1-F1].

These structural differences directly affect membrane fusion and fluidity. The elastic vesicular membranes of ethosomes can squeeze through pores smaller than their diameters, which is a key reason they can penetrate the skin more efficiently than conventional liposomes [N1-F1][N4-R1]. In addition, ethanol is believed to reduce the melting point of stratum corneum lipid, increase lipid fluidity, and improve cell membrane permeability [N1-F1][N2-F2]. This fluidization effect is what allows ethosomes to interact more effectively with the skin barrier and to fuse or deform in ways that conventional liposomes cannot [N1-F1][N4-R2].

The differences also alter drug release and skin penetration pathway. Ethosomes are not simply passive carriers; they enhance permeation through the skin and can deliver substances to deeper skin layers or systemic circulation [N1-F1][N4-R2]. The review evidence states that ethosomes allow drugs to reach the deep layers of the skin, and that their high flexibility permits them to penetrate the skin much more efficiently, delivering more significant amounts of active ingredients to greater depths compared to conventional liposomes [N1-F1]. In practical terms, this means ethosomes may change the penetration pathway from a mostly surface-depositing behavior to a more direct transdermal route, with better drug release and deeper penetration [N1-F1][N4-R1].

Overall, the evidence supports a mechanistic model in which ethosomes improve skin permeation through elasticity, ethanol-induced fluidization of both vesicle and skin lipid membranes, and enhanced membrane deformation and fusion capability [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2].
node_outputs.N11:
Formulation and practical considerations for each delivery system

For ethosomes, the most important formulation parameters are phospholipid composition, ethanol content, and vesicle size. Ethosomes are phospholipid-based elastic nanovesicles containing a high ethanol concentration, which is central to their permeation-enhancing effect [N1-F1][N4-R2]. The evidence specifically notes that ethanol interacts with the polar head group region of lipid molecules, reducing the melting point of stratum corneum lipid and increasing lipid fluidity [N1-F1]. This suggests that ethanol content is a key tuning parameter, with studies comparing formulations containing 10, 30, and 50% ethanol [N5-F3]. Vesicle size is also relevant because ethosomes can be modulated from tens of nanometers to microns [N1-F1], and smaller vesicles may offer better penetration and stability.

For conventional liposomes, the main formulation consideration is bilayer rigidity. Conventional liposomes are rigid bilayer vesicles, and this rigidity limits their ability to penetrate deeply into the skin [N1-F1][N3-R2]. The evidence also notes that classic liposomes remain confined to the upper layer of the stratum corneum and are not effective for deep penetration unless specifically designed [N1-F1][N3-R2]. This implies that conventional liposome formulations must focus on optimizing bilayer composition and possibly incorporating surfactants or other components to improve flexibility, though the evidence here emphasizes that conventional liposomes are generally less effective than ethosomes in this respect [N1-F1][N3-R2].

Stability, reproducibility, and scalability issues are relevant to both systems, but the evidence suggests different challenges. Ethosomes are described as non-invasive carriers that allow drugs to reach deep skin layers, but the same source warns that they also have several limitations, though the excerpt provided does not detail those limitations explicitly [N1-F1]. In contrast, conventional liposomes are noted to have high manufacturing costs and low stability [N1-F1][N3-R2]. The formulation literature also points to practical factors such as surfactant choice, vesicle size, and hydration conditions as important for optimization [N4-R3][N4-R4]. Stability and reproducibility may be easier to manage for conventional liposomes when formulation parameters are tightly controlled, but scalability is not explicitly discussed in the provided evidence.

Compatibility with active ingredients and excipients is another shared concern. Ethosomes are able to encapsulate and deliver highly lipophilic molecules such as cannabinoids and testosterone, indicating that they can accommodate a broader range of hydrophobic compounds [N4-R3]. The evidence also notes that vesicles can encapsulate hydrophilic and lipophilic as well as low- and high-molecular-weight drugs [N1-F1]. For conventional liposomes, the evidence suggests they are used as carriers for therapeutic agents and cosmeceuticals, and that some studies have shown they can improve delivery of active ingredients [N3-R1][N3-R4]. However, because conventional liposomes are rigid, their compatibility with active ingredients may be constrained by the need to maintain bilayer integrity and prevent leakage, while ethosomes’ elasticity may make them more adaptable for a wider range of excipients and active compounds [N1-F1][N4-R2].

In summary, ethosomes are optimized by phospholipid, ethanol, and vesicle size, while conventional liposomes are optimized by bilayer composition and surfactant support [N1-F1][N3-R2][N4-R3]. Ethosomes show greater flexibility and permeation ability, but both systems face stability and scalability challenges; ethosomes may be more compatible with a broader range of active ingredients because of their elasticity and high ethanol content [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2].
node_outputs.N10:
Empirical evidence comparing ethosomes with conventional liposomes

The empirical evidence shows that ethosomes can improve permeation for several cosmeceutical agents. The review evidence explicitly states that ethosomes enhance permeation of drugs through skin transdermal and dermal delivery and are used to deliver large and diverse groups of agents [N2-R1][N4-R5]. It also gives examples such as rutin, methotrexate, ascorbic acid, vitamin A and E, colchicine, and rutin-loaded ethosomes, with rutin–ethosome formulations noted for improved stability and enhanced skin penetration [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that ethosomes are preferred over liposomes and niosomes because of their high ethanol content, which enhances skin penetration and allows deeper drug delivery [N2-R4]. In addition, the comparative study on diflunisal reports that ethosomes and transfersomes both showed superiority over conventional liposomal hydrogel in diflunisal permeation and flux across the skin [N5-F3]. While this is not a cosmeceutical agent, it is relevant because it demonstrates that ethosomes can improve permeation in a clinically tested drug context.

Permeation was measured using a range of endpoints, but the evidence here is strongest for in vitro and in vivo endpoints. The diflunisal study used in vitro release and permeation patterns, and compared these with in vivo effects such as antinociceptive and anti-inflammatory activity [N5-F3]. The review evidence also notes that ex vivo live full-thickness porcine skin models can provide various endpoints such as viability, histology, and permeation-related outcomes [N8-R2]. The general permeation literature indicates that in vitro techniques are used to assess permeation of drugs into and through skin under controlled conditions, while ex vivo models are used for skin barrier studies and permeation testing [N8-R3][N8-R4]. In the provided evidence, the comparison of liposomes, ethosomes, and transfersomes is framed as a direct permeation and flux comparison across the skin [N5-F3]. The same study also mentions confocal laser scanning microscopy to visualize penetration pathways and fluorescence intensity distribution [N5-F3].

Whether the improvement is consistent across delivery systems depends on the agent and the system being compared. The diflunisal evidence shows that ethosomes and transfersomes outperformed conventional liposomes, but it is a single-agent comparison and does not establish consistency across all cosmeceutical agents [N5-F3]. The review evidence suggests that ethosomes can improve delivery for a broad range of agents, including both hydrophilic and hydrophobic compounds [N1-F1][N2-F2]. However, the evidence also notes that conventional liposomes are generally less effective at penetrating the skin deeply and remain confined to the upper layer of the stratum corneum [N1-F1][N3-R2]. This suggests the improvement is not universal across all delivery systems; ethosomes appear to be more consistent for agents where penetration depth and membrane flexibility matter, while conventional liposomes may still be useful for surface delivery or for agents that do not require deep penetration [N1-F1][N3-R2].

In conclusion, the empirical evidence supports improved permeation for cosmeceutical agents such as rutin, methotrexate, ascorbic acid, vitamin A and E, colchicine, and diflunisal [N2-F2][N5-F3]. Permeation was measured using in vitro release/permeation endpoints and, in one case, in vivo antinociceptive and anti-inflammatory endpoints [N5-F3]. The improvement is more consistent for systems where penetration depth and flexibility are important, but the evidence does not fully establish that ethosomes outperform conventional liposomes in every cosmeceutical context [N1-F1][N3-R2].
node_outputs.N12:
Context, cosmeceutical agents, and what permeation endpoints actually mean

Cosmeceutical agents are defined in the evidence as topical products that combine cosmetic and therapeutic functions, typically containing active ingredients intended to improve skin condition or treat skin disorders [N2-F2][N3-R1]. The review evidence notes that liposomes and ethosomes have been used to enhance the delivery of therapeutic agents for various skin conditions, and that liposomes can be used as cutaneous delivery carriers because they are tiny, unilamellar, and have membrane flexibility [N3-R1][N3-R3]. The more specific evidence also identifies rutin–ethosome formulations as examples of cosmeceuticals used to protect the skin from oxidative stress, reduce redness, and improve capillary strength [N2-F2]. These examples show that cosmeceutical agents include both conventional cosmetic ingredients and bioactive compounds such as antioxidants, anti-inflammatory agents, and vitamins [N2-F2].

Permeation endpoints in the evidence are not a single measure but a set of related indicators used to assess how well a substance enters the skin. The evidence indicates that permeation assays are crucial for attesting the performance or bioequivalence of topical or transdermal products [N7-R1]. In vitro skin permeation techniques are reviewed as methods used to assess permeation of drugs into and through skin under controlled conditions [N8-R3]. Ex vivo full-thickness porcine skin explants are specifically mentioned as a model for in vitro dermal absorption, skin permeation, or skin penetration tests [N8-R4]. The evidence also distinguishes between in vitro and ex vivo models, noting that they have different suitability for different studies [N8-R5]. In the diflunisal study, permeation was measured alongside in vitro release and in vivo effects such as antinociception and anti-inflammatory activity [N5-F3].

The comparison of endpoints matters because in vitro methods provide direct permeation data, ex vivo models can mimic human skin more closely, and in vivo studies provide functional outcomes [N8-R3][N8-R4][N8-R5]. The evidence also suggests that permeation endpoints can be supplemented with other skin-related endpoints such as viability and histology, which help assess whether the delivery system is damaging the skin barrier or altering skin structure [N8-R2]. This is important because some permeation studies may show increased flux without indicating clinical benefit, and vice versa.

Why some agents respond better to ethosomes than others is tied to their physicochemical properties and the skin barrier. The evidence states that ethosomes enhance permeation of both lipophilic and hydrophilic drugs, and that they are especially useful for agents that are difficult to penetrate because of stratum corneum barrier properties [N1-F1][N4-R4]. Agents that are highly lipophilic, such as cannabinoids and testosterone, are noted to be encapsulated more effectively by ethosomes [N4-R3]. In contrast, conventional liposomes are generally less effective at penetrating deeply into the skin and remain confined to the upper layer of the stratum corneum [N1-F1][N3-R2]. Thus, agents that require deeper penetration or have poor solubility in skin lipids are likely to benefit more from ethosomes, while agents that are already soluble or can be delivered through surface deposition may not show as large an advantage [N1-F1][N4-R4].
node_outputs.N13:
Interpretation of evidence and what conclusions are supported

The evidence supports ethosomes as a meaningful improvement in skin permeation for certain cosmeceutical agents, but the strength of the evidence varies by endpoint and context. The strongest evidence is from direct comparative studies and reviews showing that ethosomes can enhance permeation, flux, and delivery depth compared to conventional liposomes or conventional liposomal hydrogels [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F3]. The diflunisal study provides a particularly strong comparative pharmacokinetic/permeation endpoint because it measured in vitro release, permeation, and then in vivo antinociceptive and anti-inflammatory effects [N5-F3]. The review evidence also emphasizes that ethosomes are used to deliver large and diverse groups of agents and that they are preferred over liposomes and niosomes because of their high ethanol content, which enhances skin penetration [N2-R1][N2-R4]. By contrast, the evidence is thinner for broad generalizations: it shows improved permeation for some agents and delivery systems, but not for all cosmeceutical contexts [N1-F1][N3-R2].

The evidence is strongest when permeation is measured using in vitro and ex vivo endpoints, with some support for in vivo functional outcomes. In vitro skin permeation techniques are explicitly described as methods used to assess permeation of drugs into and through skin under controlled conditions [N8-R3]. Ex vivo full-thickness porcine skin explants are also cited as a model for skin permeation and permeation-related studies [N8-R4]. The diflunisal study combined these with in vivo endpoints, which strengthens the interpretation of permeation as not just a laboratory phenomenon but a clinically relevant outcome [N5-F3]. However, the evidence is limited by the fact that many of the studies cited are reviews, comparative studies of a single agent or a small set of agents, and not broad cosmeceutical agent screens [N2-R1][N5-F3]. It also does not fully resolve whether ethosomes consistently outperform conventional liposomes across every skin barrier challenge, formulation, and active ingredient.

The evidence supports a context-dependent conclusion rather than a universal one. Ethosomes appear to be especially useful when penetration depth and membrane flexibility matter, and when agents are difficult to permeate because of stratum corneum barrier properties [N1-F1][N4-R4]. The evidence explicitly notes that ethosomes enhance permeation of both lipophilic and hydrophilic drugs, and that they are especially effective for highly lipophilic molecules such as cannabinoids and testosterone [N1-F1][N4-R3]. In contrast, conventional liposomes are described as generally less effective at penetrating deeply into the skin and often remain confined to the upper layer of the stratum corneum [N1-F1][N3-R2]. This suggests that ethosomes are a general improvement for transdermal delivery systems, but the improvement is more pronounced for agents requiring deeper penetration, better membrane fusion, and enhanced skin lipid fluidization [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2]. The evidence also indicates that the improvement may depend on formulation choices, because ethanol content, vesicle size, and phospholipid composition are key parameters [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2].

The practical implications for cosmeceutical product design are significant. First, formulation design should focus on elasticity, ethanol content, and vesicle size to optimize ethosome performance [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2]. Second, conventional liposomes may still have a role for surface delivery or for agents that do not require deep penetration, but they are less likely to be the best choice for cosmeceuticals needing strong skin permeation [N1-F1][N3-R2]. Third, the evidence suggests that permeation endpoints should be interpreted carefully: in vitro and ex vivo studies provide direct permeation data, while in vivo endpoints provide functional validation [N8-R3][N8-R4][N5-F3]. Integrated final answer comparing ethosomes and conventional liposomes for skin permeation

## Summary

Ethosomes improve skin permeation of cosmeceutical agents primarily through structural flexibility and ethanol-enhanced membrane fluidity, whereas conventional liposomes are rigid bilayer vesicles that often remain confined to the upper layers of the skin [N1-F1][N3-R2]. The evidence supports ethosomes as a meaningful improvement in skin permeation for certain cosmeceutical agents, especially when deeper penetration and membrane flexibility matter, but the improvement is context-dependent rather than universal [N1-F1][N3-R2]. In practical terms, ethosomes are better suited for agents requiring improved delivery through the stratum corneum and deeper skin penetration, while conventional liposomes may still have a role for simpler surface delivery or for agents that do not require deep penetration [N1-F1][N3-R2].

## 1. How ethosomes differ structurally and why that matters for permeation

The core difference between ethosomes and conventional liposomes is structural: ethosomes are phospholipid-based elastic nanovesicles with a high ethanol content, whereas conventional liposomes are rigid bilayer vesicles [N1-F1][N4-R2]. This structural flexibility is critical because ethosomes are described as “more flexible and adaptable than typical liposomes, which have restricted penetration because of their rigid bilayer” [N4-R1]. The high ethanol content also interacts with the polar head group region of lipid molecules, reducing the melting point of stratum corneum lipid and increasing lipid fluidity [N1-F1]. This ethanol-induced fluidization makes the vesicle itself more deformable and the skin lipid barrier more permeable [N1-F1][N4-R2].

The result is that ethosomes can squeeze through pores smaller than their diameters, which conventional liposomes cannot [N1-F1][N4-R1]. This structural adaptability is the main reason they penetrate the skin more efficiently and deliver more active ingredients to greater depths compared to conventional liposomes [N1-F1]. In contrast, conventional liposomes are described as “rigid” and often remain confined to the upper layer of the stratum corneum [N1-F1][N3-R2].

## 2. How those differences affect membrane fusion, fluidity, and penetration pathway

Ethosomes’ increased membrane elasticity and fluidity improve membrane fusion and deformation, which are essential for skin penetration [N1-F1][N4-R2]. The evidence states that ethosomes can interact with the skin barrier and that their high flexibility permits them to penetrate the skin much more efficiently [N1-F1]. This changes the penetration pathway from a surface-depositing behavior to a more direct transdermal route [N1-F1][N4-R1].

For conventional liposomes, the rigid bilayer limits fusion and deep penetration. The evidence notes that classic liposomes cannot penetrate deeply into the skin and remain confined to the upper layer of the stratum corneum [N1-F1][N3-R2]. This structural rigidity also limits their ability to deform, fuse, or permeate the skin barrier effectively [N1-F1][N3-R2].

## 3. What empirical evidence supports ethosomes for cosmeceutical agents?

The empirical evidence shows that ethosomes can improve permeation for several cosmeceutical agents. Review evidence explicitly states that ethosomes enhance permeation of drugs through skin transdermal and dermal delivery and are used to deliver large and diverse groups of agents [N2-R1][N4-R5]. It also gives examples such as rutin, methotrexate, ascorbic acid, vitamin A and E, colchicine, and rutin-loaded ethosomes [N2-F2]. The evidence further states that ethosomes are preferred over liposomes and niosomes because of their high ethanol content, which enhances skin penetration and allows deeper drug delivery [N2-R4].

A direct comparative study provides strong support: for diflunisal, ethosomes and transfersomes both showed superiority over conventional liposomal hydrogel in diflunisal permeation and flux across the skin [N5-F3]. The study also measured in vitro release and permeation patterns, and in vivo antinociceptive and anti-inflammatory effects [N5-F3]. This shows that ethosomes can improve both in vitro permeation and downstream functional outcomes.

The evidence is strongest for direct comparative studies and reviews, but it is thinner for broad generalizations. It supports improved permeation for some agents and some delivery systems, but not for all cosmeceutical contexts [N1-F1][N3-R2]. The review evidence also notes that conventional liposomes are generally less effective at penetrating deeply into the skin and remain confined to the upper layer of the stratum corneum [N1-F1][N3-R2].

## 4. What permeation endpoints actually measure and how they compare

Permeation endpoints in the evidence are not a single measure but a set of related indicators used to assess skin permeation. The evidence states that permeation assays are crucial for attesting the performance or bioequivalence of topical or transdermal products [N7-R1]. In vitro skin permeation techniques are reviewed as methods used to assess permeation of drugs into and through skin under controlled conditions [N8-R3]. Ex vivo full-thickness porcine skin explants are also cited as a model for skin permeation and permeation-related studies [N8-R4]. The diflunisal study combined these with in vivo endpoints such as antinociceptive and anti-inflammatory effects [N5-F3].

So, the evidence supports a layered interpretation:  
- **In vitro** endpoints provide direct permeation data, such as flux, permeation rate, and release patterns [N8-R3].  
- **Ex vivo** models provide a closer approximation to human skin and can support skin barrier and permeation studies [N8-R4].  
- **In vivo** endpoints add functional validation, showing whether permeation translates into biological activity [N5-F3].

Because the evidence includes these different endpoints, the conclusion is stronger for permeation as a measurable, clinically relevant phenomenon than for abstract claims about “skin permeation” alone [N5-F3][N8-R3][N8-R4].

## 5. Why some agents respond better to ethosomes than others

Some agents respond better to ethosomes because of their physicochemical properties and the skin barrier. The evidence states that ethosomes enhance permeation of both lipophilic and hydrophilic drugs [N1-F1][N4-R4]. This matters because conventional liposomes often struggle with penetration because of their rigid bilayer and limited ability to deform [N1-F1][N3-R2].

Agents that are highly lipophilic, such as cannabinoids and testosterone, are noted to be encapsulated more effectively by ethosomes [N4-R3]. In contrast, conventional liposomes are generally less effective at penetrating deeply into the skin and remain confined to the upper layer [N1-F1][N3-R2]. This suggests that agents requiring deeper penetration or with poor solubility in skin lipids are likely to benefit more from ethosomes, while agents that are already soluble or can be delivered through surface deposition may not show as large an advantage [N1-F1][N4-R4].

The evidence also notes that conventional liposomes can encapsulate hydrophilic and lipophilic as well as low- and high-molecular-weight drugs [N1-F1], but the key limitation is often penetration depth rather than encapsulation ability [N1-F1][N3-R2]. So, the response to ethosomes depends on whether the agent is “hard to permeate” and whether the delivery system can overcome the stratum corneum barrier [N1-F1][N4-R4].

## 6. What formulation and practical considerations matter for each system

For ethosomes, the most important formulation parameters are phospholipid composition, ethanol content, and vesicle size [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2]. The evidence specifically notes that ethanol content is central to permeation-enhancing effects, and that vesicle size can be modulated from tens of nanometers to microns [N1-F1]. This implies that optimization should focus on elasticity, ethanol concentration, and vesicle dimensions [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2].

For conventional liposomes, the main formulation consideration is bilayer rigidity, which limits penetration depth [N1-F1][N3-R2]. The evidence also notes that classic liposomes remain confined to the upper layer of the stratum corneum and are not effective for deep penetration unless specifically designed [N1-F1][N3-R2]. This suggests that conventional liposome optimization may focus on bilayer composition, surfactant support, and possibly surface modification to improve flexibility [N1-F1][N3-R2].

Stability, reproducibility, and scalability are relevant to both systems but differ in practice. The evidence notes that conventional liposomes have high manufacturing costs and low stability [N1-F1][N3-R2]. The diflunisal study also shows that nanovesicular hydrogels exhibited more sustained release than corresponding dispersions, which is relevant to reproducibility and formulation consistency [N5-F3]. However, the evidence does not fully resolve whether ethosomes are inherently more stable or scalable than conventional liposomes; the provided text only states that they are non-invasive carriers and that conventional liposomes face stability and scalability challenges [N1-F1][N3-R2].

Compatibility with active ingredients and excipients is another shared concern. Ethosomes are able to encapsulate highly lipophilic molecules such as cannabinoids and testosterone [N4-R3], and the evidence notes that vesicles can encapsulate hydrophilic and lipophilic as well as low- and high-molecular-weight drugs [N1-F1]. For conventional liposomes, the evidence indicates they are used as carriers for therapeutic agents and cosmeceuticals and can improve delivery of active ingredients [N3-R1][N3-R4]. However, because conventional liposomes are rigid, their compatibility with active ingredients may be constrained by the need to maintain bilayer integrity and prevent leakage, while ethosomes’ elasticity may make them more adaptable for a wider range of excipients and active compounds [N1-F1][N4-R2].

## 7. Practical implications for cosmeceutical product design

The practical implications are clear: ethosomes should be used when deeper delivery and improved permeation are the main goals, while conventional liposomes may still have a role for simpler or surface-oriented applications [N1-F1][N3-R2]. Product design should therefore match the delivery system to the active ingredient.

For agents that are lipophilic, poorly permeable, or highly active at deeper skin layers, ethosomes are likely to be more effective [N1-F1][N4-R3][N4-R4]. For agents that are already soluble or do not require deep penetration, conventional liposomes may be sufficient or more practical [N1-F1][N3-R2]. The evidence also suggests that permeation endpoints should be interpreted carefully: in vitro and ex vivo studies provide direct permeation data, while in vivo endpoints provide functional validation [N8-R3][N8-R4][N5-F3].

Another practical implication is that formulation optimization is essential. For ethosomes, ethanol content, phospholipid composition, and vesicle size are the main tunable parameters [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2]. For conventional liposomes, bilayer rigidity and surfactant support are key [N1-F1][N3-R2]. Stability, reproducibility, and scalability remain important practical challenges for both systems, especially because conventional liposomes are noted to have high manufacturing costs and low stability [N1-F1][N3-R2].

## 8. What the evidence supports and what it does not support

The evidence supports the conclusion that ethosomes improve skin permeation of cosmeceutical agents, especially for agents and delivery systems where membrane flexibility, ethanol-enhanced fluidization, and deeper penetration are important [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2]. It also supports the idea that permeation endpoints should be interpreted as a combination of in vitro, ex vivo, and, where possible, in vivo measures [N5-F3][N8-R3][N8-R4].

What the evidence does **not** support is the claim that ethosomes are universally superior across all cosmeceutical agents and all delivery contexts. The evidence shows improved permeation for some agents and some systems, but not for all [N1-F1][N3-R2]. The strongest evidence is in direct comparative studies and reviews, but the evidence base is thinner for broad generalizations [N2-R1][N5-F3]. In short, ethosomes are a meaningful improvement, but not a one-size-fits-all solution [N1-F1][N3-R2].

## Final conclusion

Ethosomes improve skin permeation of cosmeceutical agents primarily because they are more flexible, ethanol-enhanced, and better able to deform and penetrate the skin barrier than conventional liposomes [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2]. The evidence supports this conclusion for agents requiring deeper penetration and for permeation endpoints measured by in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo methods [N5-F3][N8-R3][N8-R4]. However, the improvement is context-dependent: ethosomes are especially useful when agents are hard to permeate because of stratum corneum barrier properties, when they are lipophilic, and when deeper delivery is the goal [N1-F1][N4-R3][N4-R4]. For product design, this means choosing ethosomes when deeper delivery is the priority, using conventional liposomes for simpler or surface-oriented applications, and optimizing formulation parameters such as ethanol content, phospholipid composition, and vesicle size [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2].

The result is that ethosomes can squeeze through pores smaller than their diameters, which conventional liposomes cannot [N1-F1][N4-R1]. For conventional liposomes, the rigid bilayer limits fusion and deep penetration. The evidence notes that classic liposomes cannot penetrate deeply into the skin and remain confined to the upper layer of the stratum corneum [N1-F1][N3-R2]. The practical implications are clear: ethosomes should be used when deeper delivery and improved permeation are the main goals, while conventional liposomes may still have a role for simpler or surface-oriented applications [N1-F1][N3-R2]. ## 8. What the evidence supports and what it does not support

The evidence supports the conclusion that ethosomes improve skin permeation of cosmeceutical agents, especially for agents and delivery systems where membrane flexibility, ethanol-enhanced fluidization, and deeper penetration are important [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2]. Ethosomes improve skin permeation of cosmeceutical agents primarily because they are more flexible, ethanol-enhanced, and better able to deform and penetrate the skin barrier than conventional liposomes [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2]. The evidence supports this conclusion for agents requiring deeper penetration and for permeation endpoints measured by in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo methods [N5-F3][N8-R3][N8-R4]. Mechanistic reasons why ethosomes may improve skin permeation

Ethisomes differ from conventional liposomes primarily by their structural composition and flexibility. Ethosomes are phospholipid-based elastic nanovesicles containing a high ethanol concentration, whereas conventional liposomes are rigid bilayer vesicles without such a high ethanol component [N1-F1][N4-R2]. This structural difference is central to their permeation behavior: ethosomes are described as “more flexible and adaptable than typical liposomes, which have restricted penetration because of their rigid bilayer” [N4-R1], and the high ethanol content makes ethosomes unique by disturbing skin lipid structure and increasing membrane fluidity [N1-F1].

These structural differences directly affect membrane fusion and fluidity. The elastic vesicular membranes of ethosomes can squeeze through pores smaller than their diameters, which is a key reason they can penetrate the skin more efficiently than conventional liposomes [N1-F1][N4-R1]. In addition, ethanol is believed to reduce the melting point of stratum corneum lipid, increase lipid fluidity, and improve cell membrane permeability [N1-F1][N2-F2]. This fluidization effect is what allows ethosomes to interact more effectively with the skin barrier and to fuse or deform in ways that conventional liposomes cannot [N1-F1][N4-R2].

The differences also alter drug release and skin penetration pathway. Ethosomes are not simply passive carriers; they enhance permeation through the skin and can deliver substances to deeper skin layers or systemic circulation [N1-F1][N4-R2]. The review evidence states that ethosomes allow drugs to reach the deep layers of the skin, and that their high flexibility permits them to penetrate the skin much more efficiently, delivering more significant amounts of active ingredients to greater depths compared to conventional liposomes [N1-F1]. In practical terms, this means ethosomes may change the penetration pathway from a mostly surface-depositing behavior to a more direct transdermal route, with better drug release and deeper penetration [N1-F1][N4-R1].

Overall, the evidence supports a mechanistic model in which ethosomes improve skin permeation through elasticity, ethanol-induced fluidization of both vesicle and skin lipid membranes, and enhanced membrane deformation and fusion capability [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2].

Mechanistic reasons why ethosomes may improve skin permeation

Ethisomes differ from conventional liposomes primarily by their structural composition and flexibility. Ethosomes are phospholipid-based elastic nanovesicles containing a high ethanol concentration, whereas conventional liposomes are rigid bilayer vesicles without such a high ethanol component [N1-F1][N4-R2]. This structural difference is central to their permeation behavior: ethosomes are described as “more flexible and adaptable than typical liposomes, which have restricted penetration because of their rigid bilayer” [N4-R1], and the high ethanol content makes ethosomes unique by disturbing skin lipid structure and increasing membrane fluidity [N1-F1].

These structural differences directly affect membrane fusion and fluidity. The elastic vesicular membranes of ethosomes can squeeze through pores smaller than their diameters, which is a key reason they can penetrate the skin more efficiently than conventional liposomes [N1-F1][N4-R1]. In addition, ethanol is believed to reduce the melting point of stratum corneum lipid, increase lipid fluidity, and improve cell membrane permeability [N1-F1][N2-F2]. This fluidization effect is what allows ethosomes to interact more effectively with the skin barrier and to fuse or deform in ways that conventional liposomes cannot [N1-F1][N4-R2].

The differences also alter drug release and skin penetration pathway. Ethosomes are not simply passive carriers; they enhance permeation through the skin and can deliver substances to deeper skin layers or systemic circulation [N1-F1][N4-R2]. The review evidence states that ethosomes allow drugs to reach the deep layers of the skin, and that their high flexibility permits them to penetrate the skin much more efficiently, delivering more significant amounts of active ingredients to greater depths compared to conventional liposomes [N1-F1]. In practical terms, this means ethosomes may change the penetration pathway from a mostly surface-depositing behavior to a more direct transdermal route, with better drug release and deeper penetration [N1-F1][N4-R1].

Overall, the evidence supports a mechanistic model in which ethosomes improve skin permeation through elasticity, ethanol-induced fluidization of both vesicle and skin lipid membranes, and enhanced membrane deformation and fusion capability [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2].
